subject: Physics
title: Motion, Forces & Gravitation Sandbox
summary: Drive a car around a loop, test Newton's three laws of motion with crates and balls, and drop things in air and vacuum before exploring the law of universal gravitation. Predict first, then watch what really happens.

scenarios.title: The Track
scenarios.setup: A race car on a straight run-up that leads into a circular track. The odometer counts distance; the arrow shows displacement from where you started.

trials.prompt: The car drives forward 50 m along the straight. Predict the distance on the odometer and its displacement from the start.
trials.outcome: Distance 50 m, displacement 50 m.
trials.explanation: In a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are the same size.

variants.prompt: The car drives forward 50 m along the straight. Predict the distance on the odometer and its displacement from the start.
variants.outcome: Distance 50 m, displacement 50 m.
variants.explanation: In a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are the same size.

variants.prompt: The car drives forward 30 m along the straight. Predict the distance on the odometer and its displacement from the start.
variants.outcome: Distance 30 m, displacement 30 m.
variants.explanation: In a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are the same size.

variants.prompt: The car drives forward 40 m along the straight, then reverses 15 m. Predict the distance on the odometer and its displacement from the start.
variants.outcome: Distance 55 m, displacement 25 m.
variants.explanation: The odometer adds up every metre driven, in both directions (40 + 15 = 55 m). Displacement is the net change in position (40 − 15 = 25 m), because going backwards undoes part of the move.

variants.prompt: The car drives forward 35 m along the straight, then reverses 20 m. Predict the distance on the odometer and its displacement from the start.
variants.outcome: Distance 55 m, displacement 15 m.

trials.prompt: Now the car drives one complete lap of the circular track, starting from the loop entry, and stops. Predict the distance and the displacement.
trials.outcome: Distance 100 m, displacement 0 m.
trials.explanation: Displacement is a vector: the straight line from where you started to where you ended. Come back to the start and it is zero, even though the odometer shows the whole 100 m you travelled.

trials.prompt: The car drives one complete lap again at a steady pace, taking 20 s. Predict its average speed and its average velocity.
trials.outcome: Average speed 5 m/s, average velocity 0 m/s.
trials.explanation: Speed is distance over time (100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s). Velocity is displacement over time (0 m ÷ 20 s = 0 m/s). The displacement for a full lap is zero, so the average velocity is zero.

trials.prompt: Watch the car drive round the loop at a steady 5 m/s. The speedometer never changes. Is the car accelerating?
trials.outcome: Yes. The speed is steady but the velocity arrow keeps turning, so the car is accelerating towards the centre.
trials.explanation: Velocity has a direction as well as a size. Changing direction is changing velocity, and any change in velocity is acceleration, even at constant speed.

scenarios.title: The Cargo Bay
scenarios.setup: A cargo bay in three parts: a heavy crate on a rough floor and a floating crate in zero gravity (Newton's first and second laws), a pair of crates pushed apart by a spring (third law), and two balls and a Newton's cradle (momentum).

trials.prompt: You push the heavy crate (80 kg) on the floor with a force of 20 N. What happens?
trials.outcome: It does not move. The floor pushes back with exactly 20 N.
trials.explanation: Friction from the floor grows to match your push, up to a limit. While your force is below that limit the forces cancel, so the crate has no acceleration.

variants.outcome: It does not move. The floor pushes back with exactly 30 N.
variants.explanation: Friction from the floor grows to match your push, up to a limit. While your force is below that limit the forces cancel, so the crate has no acceleration.

variants.prompt: You push the heavy crate (40 kg) on the floor with a force of 300 N. What happens?
variants.outcome: It moves off and speeds up. Your 300 N beats the friction limit (about 196 N), and with sliding friction of 157 N the net force of 143 N gives it 3.6 m/s².
variants.explanation: Friction can only match your push up to a limit. Once the force is bigger than that limit it cannot balance it, so there is a net force and the crate accelerates, F = m a.

trials.prompt: You give the floating 20 kg crate a push of 40 N for 0.5 s, then let go. What does it do afterwards?

options.label: It slows down and stops soon
It keeps going at the same speed

trials.outcome: It drifts on at a constant 1 m/s and never stops by itself.
trials.explanation: Nothing pushes or drags it after the push, so there is no net force. Newton's first law: an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts. This is inertia.

trials.prompt: In zero gravity you push the 20 kg crate with a steady 40 N. Predict its acceleration.
trials.outcome: 2 m/s²: every second its speed grows by 2 m/s.

trials.prompt: A 60 kg crate and a 20 kg crate float touching in space. A spring between them pushes them apart with 30 N. Which crate feels the bigger force from the spring?

options.label: Both feel the same force, pointing in opposite directions

trials.outcome: Both feel exactly 30 N, in opposite directions. The 20 kg crate accelerates at 1.5 m/s² and the 60 kg crate at 0.5 m/s².
trials.explanation: Newton's third law: when one object pushes another, the other pushes back equally hard in the opposite direction. The forces are equal, but by F = m a the lighter crate gets the bigger acceleration.

trials.prompt: A 5 kg ball rolls at 4 m/s into a 1 kg ball that is standing still. What happens just after they collide?

options.label: They stick together and move off slowly
The moving ball slows down but keeps going forward; the other ball shoots off faster than the first was moving
The moving ball stops dead; the other ball moves off at the first ball's original speed
The moving ball bounces back; the other ball moves off forward

trials.outcome: The 5 kg ball moves at 2.7 m/s and the 1 kg ball at 6.7 m/s.
trials.explanation: Total momentum (mass × velocity) is conserved: 5 × 4 = 20 kg·m/s before, and 5 × 2.7 + 1 × 6.7 = 20 after. The moving ball hands over momentum, and a small mass needs a big speed to carry it.

trials.explanation: Momentum and energy are both conserved. Only the same number of balls leaving at the same speed conserves both; any other number would need a different speed that breaks energy conservation.

variants.prompt: A cricket fielder pulls their hands back as they catch a fast ball. Why does that help?

options.label: It makes the stopping time longer, so the force on the hands is smaller

variants.outcome: It makes the stopping time longer, so the force on the hands is smaller.
variants.explanation: The ball's momentum has to go to zero either way. A longer stopping time means a smaller force, F = change in momentum ÷ time.

trials.prompt: A rocket in empty space fires hot gas out of its engine. What pushes the rocket forwards?

options.label: The gas pushing back on the rocket
Nothing: it only moves because it is already moving

trials.outcome: The gas pushing back on the rocket.
trials.explanation: The engine pushes the gas backwards, so by the third law the gas pushes the rocket forwards with an equal force. Rockets work in a vacuum because they need nothing to push against except their own exhaust.

variants.explanation: She pushes the wall; the wall pushes her back with an equal force in the opposite direction. That reaction force is what accelerates her.

variants.prompt: A heavy rifle fires a light bullet. Compare the forces on the bullet and on the rifle while the bullet is accelerated down the barrel.

options.label: Equal in size and opposite in direction
The force on the bullet is bigger
The force on the rifle is bigger

variants.outcome: Equal in size and opposite in direction.
variants.explanation: The third law: the rifle pushes the bullet forwards and the bullet pushes the rifle backwards with exactly the same force. The light bullet accelerates much more than the heavy rifle recoils because a = F ÷ m.

variants.prompt: You blow up a balloon and let it go. It shoots across the room. What pushes the balloon forwards?

variants.outcome: The air rushing out pushes back on the balloon.
variants.explanation: The balloon pushes air out backwards, and the air pushes the balloon forwards with an equal force: action and reaction.

variants.prompt: A person stands in a small boat and throws a heavy bag out of the back. What happens to the boat?
variants.outcome: It moves forward.
variants.explanation: The person pushes the bag backwards; the bag pushes the person and boat forwards with an equal force. The third law again.

scenarios.title: The Gravity Lab

trials.prompt: Two masses attract each other with a force F = G m₁ m₂ / r². They start 3 m apart and you move them until they are 6 m apart. What happens to the force?

trials.explanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: F is proportional to 1/r². Multiplying r by 2 multiplies r² by 4, so the force is multiplied by 0.25.

laws.name: Law of inertia
laws.summary: An object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts.

laws.name: Law of acceleration
laws.summary: Acceleration is force divided by mass.

laws.name: Action and reaction
laws.summary: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

laws.name: Universal gravitation
laws.summary: Every mass attracts every other mass.
